newsitem.title: UK: Hague says well placed to win UK Tory leadership.
newsitem.headline: Hague says well placed to win UK Tory leadership.

text.p: Ex-Welsh secretary William Hague said on Tuesday his second-place finish in the initial ballot for the Conservative leadership had put him in a good position to win the contest.
"I think it's a very good result which has exceeded expectations," Hague, who was backed by 41 of the 164 Conservative MPs, said.

Hague said: "I think it puts me in a very good position to campaign for the second ballot on a platform of uniting the party and giving the party a fresh start, and I think it clearly puts me in a position to win. So we will go into the second ballot with great confidence."
Ex-finance minister Kenneth Clarke came top with 49 votes -- not enough to win outright -- and also led a consultative ballot of Conservative activists.

"I have today topped the poll in every test of Conservative opinion. I am very encouraged by the breadth of the support I have attracted, which is much stronger than I dared to expect when this campaign started," Clarke said in a statement.
"The Conservative Party should now unite to fight Labour. I intend to seek to broaden my appeal further by setting out how I intend to lead this party on an inclusive basis."
"The leadership of the party must attract and draw on the talents of every strand of opinion within the Conservative tradition," he said.

Euro-sceptic John Redwood, who came third with 27 votes, appealed to former right-wing cabinet colleagues Peter Lilley and Michael Howard, who came fourth and fifth with 24 and 23 votes respectively, to drop out of the race and give him their support.
"They will find me very generous. I want them on side and I would like them to bring as many supporters as possible," Redwood said.
"I believe there is a majority in the party for the kind of views I'm putting forward. They're not extreme right views...and I wish now to appeal across the party," Redwood said.

But Lord Jeffrey Archer, a Lilley supporter, said Redwood's narrow margin ahead of the other right-wing candidates meant nothing was certain. "I don't think it's inevitable anybody will back anybody," he said.
The second ballot will be held next Tuesday.
